directAnswer: Pope St. Zachary was a Greek-speaking churchman from Santa Severina in Calabria who led the Church from 741 to 752. He is remembered for negotiating peace with the Lombard kings, backing St. Boniface's mission in Germany, and giving the answer that cleared the way for Pepin the Short to become king of the Franks. He is generally counted as the last pope of Greek origin.

sections.h2: A Greek Pope Between Lombards and Byzantium
paras: Zachary (Zacharias) came from a Greek family in Byzantine southern Italy, at a time when many Roman clergy had roots in the Greek East. He served as a deacon in Rome and was elected within days of the death of Gregory III, apparently without waiting for confirmation from the emperor or the exarch at Ravenna. Historians often treat him as the last of the so-called Byzantine popes, the run of pontiffs of Greek or Syrian background who governed the Roman Church in the seventh and eighth centuries.

Rome was then squeezed between a distant and often hostile imperial government in Constantinople, which was pursuing iconoclasm, and the Lombard kingdom that pressed on central Italy. Zachary chose personal diplomacy. In 742 he traveled to meet King Liutprand at Terni and, according to the Liber Pontificalis, secured the return of several towns the Lombards had seized, along with a truce. He later went to Pavia to plead for Ravenna, and in 749 he persuaded King Ratchis to lift his siege of Perugia. Ratchis soon afterward abdicated and entered the monastery of Monte Cassino.

sections.h2: St. Boniface and the Reform of the Frankish Church
paras: Zachary corresponded extensively with St. Boniface, the English missionary to the Germans, and several of their letters survive. He confirmed the bishoprics Boniface founded, encouraged the reforming synods held in the Frankish lands under Carloman and Pepin, and answered detailed questions about church discipline, marriage, and the validity of baptisms performed with faulty Latin.

At a Roman synod in 745 he examined and condemned two wandering preachers, Aldebert and Clement, whom Boniface had accused of spreading error and superstition among the faithful. These contacts tied the Church north of the Alps more closely to Rome than ever before.

sections.h2: Pepin the Short and the End of the Merovingians
paras: Around 750 the Frankish mayor of the palace, Pepin, sent envoys to Rome with a pointed question: was it right that the man who held no real power should bear the title of king? The Frankish annals report that Zachary replied it was better for the one who actually ruled to be called king. With that endorsement Pepin was raised to the throne in 751, and the last Merovingian king, Childeric III, was sent to a monastery.

The episode is often seen as the beginning of the Franco-papal alliance that would shape Western Europe for centuries, although the fuller partnership was sealed under Zachary's successor, Stephen II.

Zachary translated the Dialogues of St. Gregory the Great into Greek, making the stories of Italian saints available to Eastern readers. In Rome he restored the Lateran palace and is said to have discovered the relic of the head of St. George, which he placed in the church of San Giorgio in Velabro. The emperor Constantine V granted him the estates of Ninfa and Norma south of Rome.
He died in March 752 and was buried in St. Peter's. The Church honors him as a saint, and his feast is kept on March 15.

keyFacts: Born at Santa Severina in Calabria, of Greek background
Met Lombard King Liutprand at Terni in 742 and won back captured towns
Condemned the preachers Aldebert and Clement at a Roman synod in 745
Endorsed Pepin the Short's claim to the Frankish crown (751)
Translated Gregory the Great's Dialogues into Greek
Feast day: March 15

faqs.question: Was Pope Zachary the last Greek pope?
faqs.answer: He is generally described as the last pope of Greek origin. After him the papacy was held almost entirely by men from Rome and Italy for many centuries.

faqs.question: What did Pope Zachary have to do with Pepin becoming king?
faqs.answer: When Pepin's envoys asked whether the one who held real power should be king, Zachary answered that he should. This papal approval helped legitimize the removal of the last Merovingian king in 751.

faqs.question: How did Pope Zachary help St. Boniface?
faqs.answer: He confirmed the dioceses Boniface founded in Germany, supported the Frankish reform councils, answered his questions on church discipline, and condemned the false preachers Boniface reported to Rome.

directAnswer: Pope Stephen II was a Roman deacon who reigned from 752 to 757 and turned to the Franks for protection against the Lombards. He crossed the Alps, anointed Pepin the Short and his sons, and received the lands later known as the Donation of Pepin, the foundation of the Papal States. Because an earlier pope-elect named Stephen died before consecration, he is sometimes numbered Stephen III.

sections.h2: Why He Is Sometimes Called Stephen III
paras: After Pope Zachary died in March 752, a Roman priest named Stephen was elected but died a few days later, before he could be consecrated. Medieval lists sometimes counted him as a pope and sometimes did not. The Church now omits him, so the man elected on March 26, 752, is Stephen II, but older books often call him Stephen III and shift the numbering of later Stephens accordingly.
The new pope was a Roman, raised in the Lateran household, and brother of the deacon Paul, who would succeed him as Paul I.

sections.h2: Aistulf's Threat and the Journey to Francia
paras: The Lombard king Aistulf had taken Ravenna in 751, ending the Byzantine exarchate in northern Italy, and he now demanded tribute from Rome. Appeals to Constantinople produced nothing. In late 753 Stephen set out across the Alps, the first pope to make that journey, and met King Pepin at Ponthion in January 754.

At the abbey of Saint-Denis in the summer of 754, Stephen anointed Pepin and his sons Charles (the future Charlemagne) and Carloman as kings and gave them the title of patricians of the Romans. Pepin in turn promised, at Quierzy, to restore to the pope the territories the Lombards had taken.

Pepin led armies into Italy in 754 and again in 756, forcing Aistulf to surrender the cities of the former exarchate and the Pentapolis. Rather than return them to the emperor, Pepin handed them to the pope. His envoy, Abbot Fulrad of Saint-Denis, laid the keys of the cities and the document of donation on the tomb of St. Peter.

This grant, known as the Donation of Pepin, is usually taken as the starting point of the Papal States, a temporal realm the popes would govern in central Italy until 1870. It also marked the papacy's decisive turn away from Byzantium and toward the Frankish West.

After Aistulf died in 756, Stephen supported Desiderius as the new Lombard king in exchange for promises of further cities. He also attended to Rome itself, restoring churches and caring for the poor through charitable foundations described in the Liber Pontificalis.
Stephen II died on April 26, 757, and was buried in St. Peter's. His brother Paul was chosen to succeed him.

keyFacts: Roman by birth; brother of his successor, Pope Paul I
First pope to cross the Alps, meeting Pepin at Ponthion in 754
Anointed Pepin and his sons at Saint-Denis in 754
Received the Donation of Pepin (756), basis of the Papal States
Sometimes numbered Stephen III because of an unconsecrated pope-elect

faqs.question: What was the Donation of Pepin?
faqs.answer: It was King Pepin's grant to Stephen II of the lands he had taken from the Lombards around Ravenna and the Adriatic coast. It formed the core of the Papal States.

faqs.question: Why did Stephen II go to the Franks instead of the Byzantine emperor?
faqs.answer: The emperor in Constantinople did not send help against the Lombard king Aistulf, who had captured Ravenna and threatened Rome. Stephen turned to Pepin, who had the military strength to intervene.

faqs.question: Did Stephen II crown Charlemagne?
faqs.answer: Not as emperor. In 754 he anointed the boy Charles, the future Charlemagne, together with his father Pepin and brother Carloman. The imperial coronation came in 800 under Leo III.

directAnswer: Pope St. Paul I, a Roman deacon and the younger brother of Stephen II, reigned from 757 to 767. He kept the new alliance with Pepin the Short alive, pressed the Lombard king Desiderius to honor his promises, and resisted Byzantine iconoclasm while sheltering Greek monks in Rome. He is honored as a saint.

paras: Paul had been educated at the Lateran with his brother Stephen and served as a deacon and close collaborator during Stephen's pontificate. When Stephen died in April 757, one faction supported the archdeacon Theophylact, but the majority chose Paul. He was consecrated only after the rival party gave way, and his first letters to Pepin announced his election in the manner Roman clergy had once used to inform the emperor.
That change in itself showed how far the papacy's orientation had shifted: the Frankish king, not the Byzantine court, was now Rome's chief protector.

Much of Paul's surviving correspondence, preserved in the Codex Carolinus, consists of appeals to Pepin. The Lombard king Desiderius had promised further cities to the papacy but was slow to hand them over, and at times he worked with Byzantine envoys against Rome. Paul relied on Frankish diplomatic pressure rather than another war to keep him in check.

In the East the emperor Constantine V was enforcing iconoclasm. Paul defended the veneration of images in letters and received Greek monks who fled persecution. He turned his family home into the monastery of San Silvestro in Capite and gave it to Greek-rite monks.

Lombard raids had left the catacombs outside Rome exposed and neglected. Paul moved many martyrs' relics into churches inside the walls, among them the remains of St. Petronilla, which he placed in a chapel at St. Peter's that became associated with the Frankish kings.

He also sent Pepin liturgical books, including an antiphonary and a responsorial, contributing to the spread of Roman chant and liturgy in Francia. Paul I died near St. Paul Outside the Walls in June 767. The Church venerates him as a saint, with his memory kept on June 28.

keyFacts: Younger brother and successor of Stephen II
His letters to Pepin survive in the Codex Carolinus
Founded San Silvestro in Capite in his family home for Greek monks
Moved St. Petronilla's relics to St. Peter's
Opposed the iconoclast policy of Emperor Constantine V

faqs.question: Was Pope Paul I related to another pope?
faqs.answer: Yes. He was the younger brother of Stephen II, whom he succeeded in 757. It is one of the few cases of brothers holding the papacy one after the other.

faqs.question: Why did Pope Paul I move relics from the catacombs?
faqs.answer: Lombard incursions had damaged and exposed the cemeteries outside Rome, so he transferred many martyrs' remains to churches inside the city for protection and veneration.

faqs.question: What was Paul I's stance on icons?
faqs.answer: He supported the veneration of sacred images against the iconoclast emperor Constantine V and welcomed Greek monks fleeing the persecution.

directAnswer: Pope Stephen III was a Sicilian-born cleric who came to power after a violent struggle over the papacy and reigned until January 772. He is best known for the Lateran Council of 769, which condemned the intruder Constantine, restricted papal elections to the Roman clergy, and upheld the veneration of images. He is sometimes numbered Stephen IV.

sections.h2: The Crisis That Brought Him to Office
paras: When Paul I died in 767, Toto, duke of Nepi, forced the election of his brother Constantine, a layman who was rushed through holy orders. Roman officials led by the primicerius Christopher and his son Sergius obtained Lombard help and drove Constantine out. A Lombard-backed priest named Philip was briefly installed and then removed in turn.

Christopher's party then secured the election of Stephen, a Sicilian who had come to Rome as a boy, been trained at the monastery of St. Chrysogonus, and served at the Lateran under several popes. The transition was marred by brutal reprisals: Constantine and several of his supporters were blinded. The Liber Pontificalis records these events without suggesting that Stephen ordered them, though they happened under his authority.

In April 769 Stephen convened a synod at the Lateran attended by Italian bishops and by a delegation of Frankish bishops sent by Charlemagne and Carloman. The council tried Constantine, condemned him, and declared his ordinations void.

To prevent a repeat, it decreed that only a cardinal priest or deacon of the Roman clergy could be elected pope, and that the laity, including the nobility and army, would no longer have a vote, though they could acclaim the one chosen. The council also affirmed the veneration of holy images and rejected the iconoclast council held at Hieria in 754.

sections.h2: Shifting Alliances and a Bitter End
paras: In his last years Stephen moved closer to the Lombard king Desiderius, and in 771 the officials Christopher and Sergius, who had made him pope, were seized and killed after falling out with the papal chamberlain Paul Afiarta and his Lombard allies. Stephen's role in their fall remains debated by historians.

He also wrote strongly against a proposed marriage between a Frankish king and Desiderius's daughter. Stephen died in January 772, leaving the papacy to Adrian I, who would break decisively with the Lombards.

keyFacts: Born in Sicily; trained at the monastery of St. Chrysogonus in Rome
Succeeded after the intrusion of the antipope Constantine
Held the Lateran Council of April 769 with Frankish bishops present
The council limited papal eligibility to Roman cardinal priests and deacons
Sometimes numbered Stephen IV

faqs.question: What did the Lateran Council of 769 decide?
faqs.answer: It condemned the antipope Constantine, required that the pope be chosen from the Roman cardinal priests or deacons, removed the laity's vote in papal elections, and upheld the veneration of sacred images.

faqs.question: Why is Stephen III also called Stephen IV?
faqs.answer: An earlier pope-elect named Stephen died in 752 before consecration. Lists that counted him shift the numbering of every later Stephen up by one.

faqs.question: Who was the antipope Constantine?
faqs.answer: He was a layman forced onto the papal throne in 767 by his brother, the duke of Nepi. He was deposed in 768 and condemned by Stephen III's council in 769.

directAnswer: Pope Adrian I was a Roman nobleman who reigned from 772 to 795, one of the longest pontificates in history. He called on Charlemagne to end the Lombard threat, sent legates to the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, which restored the veneration of icons, and rebuilt much of Rome's walls, aqueducts, and churches.

sections.h2: Charlemagne and the Fall of the Lombard Kingdom
paras: Adrian came from a prominent Roman family and had been raised in the household of his uncle after his parents died young. Soon after his election the Lombard king Desiderius seized papal towns and advanced toward Rome. Adrian appealed to Charlemagne, who crossed the Alps in 773 and besieged Pavia.

During the siege Charlemagne visited Rome for Easter 774, where Adrian received him at St. Peter's and the king confirmed his father's donation of lands to the papacy. Pavia fell soon after, Desiderius was sent to a Frankish monastery, and Charlemagne took the title King of the Lombards. The partnership between pope and king defined the rest of Adrian's reign.

In Constantinople the empress Irene, acting for her young son, moved to end the first period of iconoclasm. Adrian sent legates to the council that met at Nicaea in 787, now counted as the seventh ecumenical council by both Catholics and Orthodox. The council taught that holy images may be venerated, while worship in the strict sense belongs to God alone.

Charlemagne's theologians, working from a poor Latin translation of the acts, criticized the council in the treatise known as the Libri Carolini, and the Frankish Council of Frankfurt in 794 voiced similar objections. Adrian defended Nicaea in a reply to the king without breaking their alliance. The same Frankfurt council, with papal support, condemned the Adoptionist teaching associated with Elipandus of Toledo and Felix of Urgell.

Adrian invested heavily in the city. He repaired the Aurelian walls and restored several aqueducts that had fallen out of use, renovated many churches, and organized papal farming estates in the countryside, called domuscultae, to feed Rome's poor.
He also sent Charlemagne a collection of church law, the Dionysio-Hadriana, which became a standard canonical reference in the Frankish kingdom.

sections.h2: A Pope Mourned by a King
paras: Adrian died on Christmas Day 795 after nearly twenty-four years as pope, a length not exceeded until the eighteenth century. Charlemagne grieved for him and had an epitaph composed, traditionally attributed to Alcuin, carved on black marble in Francia and sent to Rome. The inscription still survives in the portico of St. Peter's Basilica.

keyFacts: Reigned almost 24 years, from 772 to 795
Called Charlemagne into Italy; the Lombard kingdom fell in 774
Sent legates to the Second Council of Nicaea (787), the seventh ecumenical council
Sent Charlemagne the Dionysio-Hadriana collection of canon law
His marble epitaph from Charlemagne survives at St. Peter's

faqs.question: What did the Second Council of Nicaea teach?
faqs.answer: Meeting in 787 with Adrian I's legates present, it affirmed that sacred images may be honored and venerated, distinguishing this from the adoration owed to God alone, and ended the first wave of iconoclasm.

faqs.question: How was Adrian I connected to Charlemagne?
faqs.answer: Adrian asked Charlemagne for help against the Lombards. Charlemagne conquered their kingdom in 774, confirmed papal lands, and remained a close ally; he even commissioned Adrian's epitaph.

faqs.question: Was Adrian I's pontificate unusually long?
faqs.answer: Yes. At nearly twenty-four years, it was the longest papal reign for about a thousand years, until Pius VI surpassed it in the late eighteenth century.

directAnswer: Pope St. Leo III, a Roman cleric of modest background, reigned from 795 to 816. After surviving a violent attack in 799, he crowned Charlemagne emperor in St. Peter's on Christmas Day 800, an act that laid the groundwork for the medieval Western empire. He was added to the Roman Martyrology in 1673.

paras: Leo had served as a cardinal priest and in the papal household before his election the day after Adrian I's death. He lacked the aristocratic connections of his predecessor, and Adrian's relatives in the papal administration resented him. On April 25, 799, during a procession, a band led by the officials Paschalis and Campulus attacked Leo, tried to blind him and cut out his tongue, and shut him in a monastery.
Leo escaped and made his way to Charlemagne at Paderborn. The king had him escorted back to Rome while Frankish envoys looked into the charges his enemies were making against him.

Charlemagne came to Rome in late 800. In December, Leo publicly swore an oath of purgation affirming his innocence, and the accusers were condemned. Then, at Mass in St. Peter's on Christmas Day, Leo placed a crown on Charlemagne's head and the assembled Romans acclaimed him emperor.

The event revived the title of emperor in the West for the first time since the fifth century. Byzantium regarded it as a usurpation, and historians still debate how far Charlemagne expected or welcomed it. In the long run it set a precedent that Western emperors received their crown from the pope.

Frankish churches had begun singing the Nicene Creed with the phrase that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son (filioque). When a Frankish delegation raised the matter in 810, Leo accepted the doctrine but refused to add the word to the Creed as used in Rome. According to the Liber Pontificalis he had the Creed in its original form engraved on silver shields placed in St. Peter's.

Leo enriched Rome's churches with gifts recorded in detail by the Liber Pontificalis and built a great hall at the Lateran decorated with mosaics showing Christ commissioning the apostles and St. Peter honoring Leo and Charlemagne. A later copy of the mosaic can still be seen near the Lateran.

After Charlemagne died in 814, a new conspiracy arose and Leo had its leaders executed, a harsh response that drew criticism. He died on June 12, 816. He was included in the Roman Martyrology in 1673, and his feast is June 12.

keyFacts: Survived an assault by Roman officials on April 25, 799
Crowned Charlemagne emperor on Christmas Day 800 in St. Peter's
Refused to add the filioque to the Creed in Rome while accepting the doctrine
Built the Lateran triclinium with its famous mosaics
Added to the Roman Martyrology in 1673; feast June 12

faqs.question: Why did Pope Leo III crown Charlemagne?
faqs.answer: Charlemagne was the most powerful ruler in the West and had restored Leo after his enemies attacked him. Crowning him emperor recognized that power and tied the new empire to the Roman Church.

faqs.question: What happened to Leo III in 799?
faqs.answer: Relatives of Adrian I attacked him during a procession, tried to mutilate him, and imprisoned him. He escaped to Charlemagne and returned to Rome under Frankish protection.

faqs.question: Did Leo III accept the filioque?
faqs.answer: He accepted the teaching that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son but declined to insert the word into the Creed used in Rome.

directAnswer: Pope Stephen IV was a Roman deacon who reigned only seven months, from June 816 to January 817. His main act was traveling to Reims, where he crowned and anointed the emperor Louis the Pious, Charlemagne's son. He is sometimes called Stephen V.

paras: Stephen came from a noble Roman family and had been raised at the Lateran, serving as a deacon under Leo III. He was elected within days of Leo's death. Mindful of the tensions that had surrounded his predecessor, he had the Romans swear loyalty to the Frankish emperor and sent word of his election to Louis.
He is also reported to have released and recalled people exiled after the conspiracies of Leo III's last years, an effort at reconciliation in a divided city.

In the autumn of 816 Stephen crossed the Alps and met Louis the Pious at Reims. There, in October, he anointed Louis and crowned him and his wife Ermengarde. Louis had already been crowned co-emperor by his father in 813 without papal involvement, so the ceremony at Reims added a religious consecration to an existing title.

Some accounts say Stephen brought a crown said to have belonged to Constantine, though this may be later embellishment. Louis confirmed the privileges of the Roman Church before the pope returned to Italy. Stephen died in January 817, a few months after coming back, and little else is recorded of his short reign.

keyFacts: Roman nobleman, deacon under Leo III
Reigned about seven months (816–817)
Anointed and crowned Louis the Pious and Empress Ermengarde at Reims in 816
Sometimes numbered Stephen V

faqs.question: Which emperor did Stephen IV crown?
faqs.answer: He crowned Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, at Reims in October 816, along with Louis's wife Ermengarde.

faqs.question: Why is so little known about Stephen IV?
faqs.answer: His pontificate lasted only about seven months, and the sources focus almost entirely on his trip to Francia for the coronation of Louis the Pious.

directAnswer: Pope St. Paschal I, a Roman monk and abbot, reigned from 817 to 824. He obtained the Pactum Ludovicianum confirming papal lands, crowned Lothair I as co-emperor, and is remembered above all as a builder: Santa Prassede, Santa Cecilia in Trastevere, and Santa Maria in Domnica still display the mosaics he commissioned.

paras: Paschal, son of Bonosus and Theodora, was a Roman cleric who had led the monastery of St. Stephen near St. Peter's, which cared for pilgrims. He was elected the day after Stephen IV died and consecrated before the emperor could confirm the choice, then sent an embassy to Louis the Pious to explain.

In 817 Louis issued the Pactum Ludovicianum, a privilege confirming the territories of the Roman Church and recognizing the freedom of papal elections. In 823 Paschal crowned Louis's son Lothair as co-emperor in Rome, strengthening the custom that imperial coronation belonged to the pope.

sections.h2: The Mosaic Churches of Paschal I
paras: Paschal's most lasting legacy is visible today. He rebuilt Santa Prassede near St. Mary Major and added the Chapel of St. Zeno, its walls covered in gold-ground mosaics; one image shows his mother Theodora with a square halo, the sign of a living person, and the label episcopa. He also rebuilt Santa Maria in Domnica on the Caelian Hill, whose apse mosaic shows Paschal kneeling at the feet of the Virgin and Child.

In Trastevere he rebuilt the basilica of Santa Cecilia. The Liber Pontificalis relates that after a long search he found the body of St. Cecilia in a catacomb along the Appian Way and translated it to her church, together with the remains of companions associated with her. Paschal transferred many other martyrs' relics into Roman churches as well.

Paschal welcomed Greek monks fleeing the renewed iconoclasm of Emperor Leo V. Late in his reign two pro-Frankish officials, Theodore and Leo, were blinded and beheaded at the Lateran. Imperial envoys investigated, and Paschal swore an oath that he had not ordered the killings, while maintaining that the victims had been guilty of treason.
He died in February 824 amid local hostility; the Liber Pontificalis is silent on the details. He was nevertheless venerated as a saint in Rome, and the churches he built remain his best memorial.

keyFacts: Former abbot of the monastery of St. Stephen by St. Peter's
Received the Pactum Ludovicianum from Louis the Pious (817)
Crowned Lothair I co-emperor in 823
Built or rebuilt Santa Prassede, Santa Cecilia in Trastevere, and Santa Maria in Domnica
Translated the relics of St. Cecilia to her basilica

faqs.question: Where can you see Pope Paschal I's mosaics today?
faqs.answer: In Rome at Santa Prassede (including the Chapel of St. Zeno), Santa Maria in Domnica, and Santa Cecilia in Trastevere. Several of the apse mosaics show Paschal himself with the square halo of a living donor.

faqs.question: Did Paschal I find St. Cecilia's body?
faqs.answer: According to the Liber Pontificalis, he located her remains in a catacomb on the Appian Way and moved them to the rebuilt basilica of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere.

faqs.question: What was the Pactum Ludovicianum?
faqs.answer: It was a privilege issued by Emperor Louis the Pious in 817 that confirmed the lands held by the Roman Church and acknowledged the freedom of papal elections.

directAnswer: Pope Eugene II was a Roman archpriest who reigned from 824 to 827. His election was disputed, and early in his reign the co-emperor Lothair imposed the Constitutio Romana, which gave the Frankish emperors oversight of papal government. In 826 he held a Roman synod remembered for its decrees on clerical discipline and schooling.

sections.h2: A Contested Election and the Constitutio Romana
paras: Eugene had been archpriest of Santa Sabina on the Aventine. After Paschal I died, the clergy and the Roman nobility split over his successor, and Eugene, the candidate of the nobles, prevailed with help from Wala, a cousin and adviser of the Frankish emperors. A rival candidate's name is given in some sources as Zinzinnus.

Lothair came to Rome in 824 and issued the Constitutio Romana. It required that a newly elected pope swear an oath of loyalty in the presence of an imperial envoy before consecration, set up imperial and papal officials to oversee justice in Rome, and guaranteed protection to those under the emperor's safeguard. For decades it shaped relations between Rome and the Carolingians.

In November 826 Eugene presided over a synod in Rome that issued a long series of canons. They addressed the conduct and education of the clergy, forbade simony, and called for schools to teach letters and doctrine at bishops' churches and other suitable places.

Eugene also received Frankish envoys concerned with the question of images after the Synod of Paris in 825, though little is known of his answer. He died in August 827. Beyond these events, the record of his pontificate is thin.

keyFacts: Former archpriest of Santa Sabina in Rome
Accepted the Constitutio Romana issued by Lothair in 824
Held a reforming synod in Rome in November 826
The synod called for schools attached to bishops' churches

faqs.question: What was the Constitutio Romana?
faqs.answer: It was a decree of Emperor Lothair in 824 that required popes to swear loyalty before an imperial envoy before consecration and established imperial supervision of justice in Rome.

faqs.question: What did Eugene II's synod of 826 accomplish?
faqs.answer: It passed canons on clerical discipline, condemned simony, and encouraged schools for teaching letters and Christian doctrine attached to bishops' churches.

directAnswer: Pope Valentine was a Roman cleric who reigned for only about a month or six weeks in late 827. He had been archdeacon under Eugene II, and the Liber Pontificalis praises his piety and learning, but almost nothing is known of what he did as pope.

paras: Valentine was born in Rome, the son of a man named Leontius from the Via Lata district. The Liber Pontificalis says he was trained at the Lateran from youth, was ordained deacon by Paschal I, and was made archdeacon by Eugene II, who reportedly held him in great affection.

After Eugene's death in August 827, the clergy, nobles, and people are said to have chosen Valentine unanimously. His biography is short and admiring, describing his chaste life and generosity, but it reports no specific decisions, councils, or buildings from his time as pope.

Valentine died roughly forty days after his elevation, and the exact length of his reign is uncertain; the dates in the papal lists are approximate. He should not be confused with St. Valentine of February 14, the earlier Roman martyr who was not a pope.
His brief tenure left the field open for Gregory IV, whose election followed after a delay while imperial approval was sought.

keyFacts: Roman by birth, son of Leontius
Archdeacon under Eugene II
Reigned only about 30 to 40 days in 827
Not the same person as the martyr St. Valentine

faqs.question: Is Pope Valentine the St. Valentine of Valentine's Day?
faqs.answer: No. The St. Valentine honored on February 14 was an early Christian martyr. Pope Valentine lived in the ninth century and is not venerated as a saint.

faqs.question: How long was Pope Valentine pope?
faqs.answer: Only around a month or six weeks in the autumn of 827; the sources give approximate dates.

directAnswer: Pope Gregory IV was a Roman cardinal priest who reigned from 827 to 844, a period dominated by civil war among the sons of Louis the Pious. He is remembered for his ill-fated attempt to mediate at the Field of Lies in 833, for fortifying Ostia against Saracen raiders, and for rebuilding parts of St. Peter's, where he moved the body of St. Gregory the Great.

paras: Gregory had been cardinal priest of San Marco, a church he later rebuilt and decorated with an apse mosaic that still survives. Chosen after the brief reign of Valentine, he was not consecrated until an imperial envoy had approved the election, in keeping with the Constitutio Romana of 824. His pontificate is a clear example of how closely papal affairs were now bound to the Carolingian court.

In 833 the sons of Louis the Pious rebelled against their father. Gregory crossed the Alps with Lothair, hoping to restore peace within the imperial family. Bishops loyal to Louis protested his presence and even threatened to depose him if he excommunicated anyone on Lothair's side, to which Gregory replied by defending the authority of the Apostolic See.

When the armies faced each other near Colmar in Alsace, Louis's supporters deserted him overnight, and he was forced to surrender. The place became known as the Field of Lies. Gregory returned to Rome with his prestige damaged, having appeared to serve as a tool of the rebels rather than as a neutral peacemaker. Louis was restored the following year.

sections.h2: Ostia, St. Peter's, and All Saints
paras: Muslim raiders from North Africa and Sicily were a growing danger to the Italian coast. Gregory rebuilt and fortified Ostia at the mouth of the Tiber, naming the new stronghold Gregoriopolis. At St. Peter's he carried out extensive works and transferred the remains of St. Gregory the Great to a new chapel in the basilica.

He is also associated with the spread of the feast of All Saints on November 1: in 835, with his encouragement, Louis the Pious extended the celebration throughout the Frankish lands. Gregory died in January 844.

keyFacts: Formerly cardinal priest of San Marco, whose apse mosaic he commissioned
Traveled with Lothair to the Field of Lies in Alsace in 833
Fortified Ostia as Gregoriopolis against Saracen raids
Moved the body of St. Gregory the Great within St. Peter's
Linked to the spread of the November 1 feast of All Saints in Francia

faqs.question: What was the Field of Lies?
faqs.answer: It was the place near Colmar where, in 833, the army of Louis the Pious deserted him for his rebellious sons. Gregory IV had come hoping to mediate, but the outcome made him look like a partisan of the rebels.

faqs.question: Did Gregory IV establish All Saints' Day?
faqs.answer: The feast already existed in Rome. Gregory IV is associated with its extension to the whole Frankish empire on November 1, decreed by Louis the Pious in 835.

faqs.question: What was Gregoriopolis?
faqs.answer: It was the fortified settlement Gregory IV built at Ostia, at the mouth of the Tiber, to protect Rome from raiders arriving by sea.

directAnswer: Pope Sergius II was an elderly Roman aristocrat who reigned from 844 to 847. Consecrated without imperial approval, he faced a Frankish army sent to assert the emperor's rights, and his reign ended in the shadow of the Saracen raid of 846 that plundered St. Peter's and St. Paul's outside the walls.

sections.h2: A Disputed Start and Frankish Pressure
paras: Sergius came from a noble Roman family and had been archpriest before his election. A deacon named John was briefly pushed forward by a popular faction and occupied the Lateran, but the nobility prevailed and installed Sergius, who intervened to spare his rival's life.

Because Sergius was consecrated without waiting for the emperor's envoys, Lothair sent his son Louis II with an army and Bishop Drogo of Metz to Rome in 844. After negotiations Sergius secured the withdrawal of the troops, crowned Louis king of the Lombards, and named Drogo papal vicar in the Frankish lands, while the Romans renewed their oath to Lothair.

The Liber Pontificalis is critical of Sergius's last years, blaming his ill health and the influence of his brother Benedict, who is accused of selling church offices. In August 846 an Arab fleet entered the Tiber. Unable to breach the city walls, the raiders sacked the basilicas of St. Peter and St. Paul, which stood outside the defenses, and carried off their treasures.
The shock of this attack prompted the building of the Leonine Wall under his successor. Sergius died in January 847, and little more about his personal role is recorded.

keyFacts: Roman noble and former archpriest
Consecrated without imperial approval, prompting Louis II's arrival in 844
Crowned Louis II king of the Lombards
Saracen raiders sacked St. Peter's and St. Paul's in August 846

faqs.question: What happened to St. Peter's Basilica under Sergius II?
faqs.answer: In August 846 Arab raiders who had sailed up the Tiber plundered St. Peter's and St. Paul's, which lay outside Rome's walls. The disaster led to the construction of the Leonine Wall.

faqs.question: Why did the Franks send an army to Rome in 844?
faqs.answer: Sergius II had been consecrated without imperial confirmation, contrary to the Constitutio Romana. Emperor Lothair sent his son Louis II to reassert imperial rights.

directAnswer: Pope St. Leo IV was a Roman of Lombard descent and a Benedictine monk who reigned from 847 to 855. Elected after the Saracen sack of St. Peter's, he enclosed the Vatican within the Leonine Wall, rallied the Italian coastal cities to victory at the Battle of Ostia in 849, and received the young Alfred of Wessex in Rome.

sections.h2: A Monk Chosen in a Crisis
paras: Leo, son of Radoald, was educated at the monastery of St. Martin near St. Peter's and later served as cardinal priest of the Santi Quattro Coronati. When Sergius II died in early 847, Rome was still reeling from the raid that had stripped St. Peter's. Leo was elected unanimously and, given the danger, was consecrated without waiting for imperial confirmation, though the clergy stated that the emperor's rights were not meant to be slighted.

In 849 a new Saracen fleet threatened the Tiber. Leo organized a league with the maritime cities of Naples, Amalfi, and Gaeta, whose ships gathered at Ostia. The pope went to bless the fleet before the battle. A storm scattered the enemy and the allied ships finished the victory; many prisoners were put to work on Rome's defenses.
Centuries later Raphael painted the Battle of Ostia in the Vatican rooms, giving Leo IV the features of Pope Leo X.

Leo's greatest work was a defensive wall around the Vatican hill and St. Peter's, a project discussed under his predecessor and financed with help from the emperor Lothair. Completed and solemnly dedicated in 852, the wall enclosed the area that became known as the Leonine City. Stretches of it can still be seen today, including the line later used by the Passetto connecting the Vatican to Castel Sant'Angelo.
Leo also restored the damaged basilicas, repaired the city's walls and gates, and founded a fortified town for refugees near Centumcellae (modern Civitavecchia), called Leopolis.

In 853 King Æthelwulf of Wessex sent his young son Alfred to Rome. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says Leo anointed him as king; modern historians generally think the pope invested the boy with the honors of a Roman consul, which English tradition later remembered as a royal anointing.

Leo held synods in Rome, including one in 853 that issued disciplinary canons and condemned the cardinal priest Anastasius, later known as the Librarian, for abandoning his church. A popular story, depicted by Raphael in the Fire in the Borgo, tells that Leo halted a fire near St. Peter's by making the sign of the cross; it is a legend rather than documented history. Leo died in July 855 and is venerated as a saint, with his feast on July 17.

keyFacts: Benedictine monk trained at St. Martin's monastery near St. Peter's
Allied with Naples, Amalfi, and Gaeta to win the Battle of Ostia (849)
Built and dedicated the Leonine Wall around the Vatican in 852
Received young Alfred of Wessex in Rome in 853
Feast day: July 17

faqs.question: What is the Leonine City?
faqs.answer: It is the area around St. Peter's and the Vatican hill that Leo IV enclosed with walls, dedicated in 852, after Saracen raiders had plundered the basilica in 846.

faqs.question: Did Pope Leo IV crown Alfred the Great?
faqs.answer: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says he anointed the boy Alfred as king in 853, but most historians believe Leo conferred the honors of a Roman consul, which was later remembered as a royal anointing.

faqs.question: Did Leo IV really stop a fire with the sign of the cross?
faqs.answer: That account is a pious legend, made famous by Raphael's fresco The Fire in the Borgo. It is not supported by contemporary evidence.

directAnswer: Pope Benedict III was a Roman cleric who reigned from 855 to 858. His election was briefly overturned when imperial envoys installed Anastasius the Librarian as antipope, but the Roman clergy and people held firm and Benedict was consecrated. He later became the pope around whom the medieval legend of Pope Joan was placed.

paras: Benedict, cardinal priest of San Callisto, was chosen after Leo IV's death in July 855. The Roman clergy sent the election decree to the emperors Lothair and Louis II, but the envoys who came back favored Anastasius, a learned cleric whom Leo IV had excommunicated. With their support Anastasius seized the Lateran, had Benedict stripped of his vestments, and held him under guard.

Clergy and people refused to accept the intruder. After several days the imperial envoys gave way, Anastasius was expelled, and Benedict was consecrated in St. Peter's on September 29, 855. He treated his rival leniently; Anastasius later returned to papal service and became one of the most learned figures of his age.

sections.h2: A Quiet Reign and a Later Legend
paras: The surviving record of Benedict's pontificate is modest. He repaired churches damaged in the Saracen raids, corresponded about disputes in the Frankish Church, and received King Æthelwulf of Wessex, who visited Rome with his son Alfred in 855 and made generous gifts. He died in April 858.

Centuries afterward, chroniclers inserted a fictional woman pope, Pope Joan, between Leo IV and Benedict III. Historians reject the story completely: contemporary sources show Benedict was elected only weeks after Leo's death, leaving no gap for another pontificate.

keyFacts: Former cardinal priest of San Callisto
Briefly displaced by the antipope Anastasius the Librarian in 855
Consecrated on September 29, 855
Received King Æthelwulf of Wessex in Rome

faqs.question: Who was Anastasius the Librarian?
faqs.answer: A highly educated Roman cleric who was set up as antipope against Benedict III in 855 with imperial backing. He was soon removed, and later served the popes as a scholar and translator.

faqs.question: Was there a Pope Joan before Benedict III?
faqs.answer: No. The Pope Joan story is a medieval legend. The sources show Benedict III was elected shortly after Leo IV's death, so there was no room for an unrecorded pontificate.

directAnswer: Pope St. Nicholas I, called the Great, reigned from 858 to 867 and is one of only three popes commonly given that title. He insisted on papal authority over powerful bishops and kings, opposed the elevation of Photius in Constantinople, refused to allow King Lothair II to set aside his lawful wife, and sent the Bulgarians a famous set of answers on Christian life.

sections.h2: A Roman Deacon Formed in the Papal Service
paras: Nicholas was the son of a Roman official and served in the papal administration under Sergius II, Leo IV, and Benedict III, who relied on him closely. Elected in April 858 in the presence of Emperor Louis II, he brought to the office a strong conviction that the Apostolic See was the final judge in matters of faith and church discipline, and he acted on it with unusual energy.
He is honored, with Leo I and Gregory I, as one of the popes known as the Great.

In 858 Patriarch Ignatius of Constantinople was forced out and replaced by Photius, a brilliant layman raised to the patriarchate within days. Nicholas sent legates to investigate; at a council in Constantinople in 861 they agreed to Photius's position, exceeding their instructions. Nicholas repudiated them and, at a Roman synod in 863, declared Photius deposed and Ignatius the rightful patriarch.

Relations worsened over the conversion of Bulgaria and over Western customs, including the filioque. In 867 Photius held a synod that claimed to depose Nicholas, but within weeks a palace coup in Constantinople removed Photius, and Nicholas died before news of the reversal could fully reach him. The dispute is a milestone in the growing estrangement between Rome and Constantinople.

sections.h2: Lothair II and the Indissolubility of Marriage
paras: King Lothair II of Lotharingia sought to repudiate his wife Theutberga in order to marry Waldrada, and a synod at Metz in 863 approved the plan. Nicholas annulled the synod's decision and deposed the archbishops Gunther of Cologne and Theutgaud of Trier, who had promoted it.

He held to this position despite military pressure from Lothair's brother, Emperor Louis II, who briefly occupied Rome. The case became a lasting example of a pope defending the rights of a wife and the permanence of marriage against royal power.

Khan Boris I of Bulgaria, newly baptized, turned to Rome in 866 with a long list of questions. Nicholas's reply, known as the Responsa ad consulta Bulgarorum, addressed more than a hundred points on baptism, fasting, marriage, justice, and the treatment of prisoners. It is valued for its pastoral moderation, for instance in condemning torture to extract confessions and rejecting forced conversion.

Nicholas also asserted the right of bishops to appeal to Rome, notably in the case of Bishop Rothad of Soissons against Archbishop Hincmar of Reims. He died on November 13, 867, and is venerated as a saint, with his feast on November 13.

keyFacts: One of three popes commonly called the Great, with Leo I and Gregory I
Declared Photius deposed at a Roman synod in 863
Annulled the Synod of Metz (863) that approved Lothair II's divorce
Sent the Responsa ad consulta Bulgarorum to Boris I in 866
Feast day: November 13

faqs.question: Why is Nicholas I called the Great?
faqs.answer: He firmly upheld the authority of the papacy over bishops, patriarchs, and kings, and defended moral and canonical principles under heavy pressure, earning him the title shared only with Leo I and Gregory I.

faqs.question: What was Nicholas I's role in the Photian Schism?
faqs.answer: He refused to recognize Photius as patriarch of Constantinople after Ignatius was forced out, and a Roman synod under him declared Photius deposed in 863.

faqs.question: What are the Responses to the Bulgarians?
faqs.answer: A detailed letter Nicholas sent in 866 to Boris I of Bulgaria, answering over a hundred questions about Christian practice and urging mercy, including a rejection of torture.

directAnswer: Pope Adrian II was a Roman priest elected at the age of about seventy-five, who reigned from 867 to 872. He welcomed Sts. Cyril and Methodius to Rome, approved the use of Slavonic in the liturgy, and confirmed the Fourth Council of Constantinople, which condemned Photius. His reign was also marked by a personal tragedy in his own family.

sections.h2: An Elderly Pope With a Family
paras: Adrian is said to have belonged to the same Roman family as Popes Stephen IV and Sergius II. He had married before ordination, as was then permitted, and had a wife, Stephania, and a daughter. He had twice declined the papacy before accepting it in December 867, chosen for his charity and moderation.

Early in 868 his wife and daughter were abducted and then killed by Eleutherius, a brother of Anastasius the Librarian. Eleutherius was executed by imperial authorities. Adrian nonetheless retained Anastasius in his service.

sections.h2: Cyril, Methodius, and the Slavonic Liturgy
paras: The brothers Cyril and Methodius, missionaries to the Slavs of Great Moravia, arrived in Rome late in 867 bringing relics believed to be those of Pope St. Clement I. Adrian received them warmly, approved their Slavonic liturgical books, and had them placed on the altar of St. Mary Major. Slavonic Masses were celebrated in several Roman churches.

Cyril died in Rome in February 869 and was buried in the basilica of San Clemente. Adrian then consecrated Methodius archbishop with jurisdiction over Pannonia and Moravia, centered on the ancient see of Sirmium, giving the Slavic mission an institutional foundation.

With the deposition of Photius in 867, the new emperor Basil I sought reconciliation with Rome. A Roman synod in 869 confirmed the condemnation of Photius, and papal legates presided at a council in Constantinople in 869 and 870 that restored Ignatius as patriarch. The Catholic Church counts this assembly as the eighth ecumenical council.

Immediately afterward, however, the Byzantines assigned the newly converted Bulgarians to the jurisdiction of Constantinople, over the protests of the papal legates, a significant loss for Rome. In the West Adrian dealt with Lothair II's marriage case and with the division of Lothair's kingdom after his death in 869. Adrian died in December 872.

keyFacts: Married before ordination; his wife and daughter were killed in 868
Approved Slavonic liturgical books for Cyril and Methodius
Consecrated Methodius archbishop for Pannonia and Moravia
Confirmed the Fourth Council of Constantinople (869–870)
Bulgaria was placed under Constantinople's jurisdiction in 870

faqs.question: How did Adrian II support Sts. Cyril and Methodius?
faqs.answer: He received them in Rome, approved their Slavonic liturgical books, allowed Slavonic Masses in Roman churches, and made Methodius an archbishop to lead the mission.

faqs.question: Was Pope Adrian II married?
faqs.answer: Yes. He married before receiving holy orders. His wife Stephania and their daughter were murdered in 868 by Eleutherius, brother of Anastasius the Librarian.

faqs.question: Which council took place under Adrian II?
faqs.answer: The Fourth Council of Constantinople (869–870), considered the eighth ecumenical council by the Catholic Church, which condemned Photius and restored Patriarch Ignatius.

directAnswer: Pope John VIII, a Roman archdeacon, reigned from 872 to 882. He crowned two Carolingian emperors, struggled to defend Rome against Saracen attacks, upheld St. Methodius and the Slavonic liturgy, and recognized Photius as patriarch after Ignatius's death. According to the Annals of Fulda, he was murdered, making him the first pope recorded as assassinated.

paras: John had served the Roman Church for decades before becoming pope. When Emperor Louis II died in 875 without a son, John chose Charles the Bald, king of the West Franks, and crowned him emperor in Rome on Christmas Day 875, hoping for a protector against the Saracens.

Charles provided little help and died in 877. After years of uncertainty, John crowned Charles the Fat emperor in 881. At home he faced opposition from Roman factions; in 876 he condemned several leading clerics, including Bishop Formosus of Porto, who fled the city.

Arab raiders established bases in southern Italy and attacked the countryside around Rome. John built a papal fleet, personally led an expedition that defeated raiders off Cape Circeo, and fortified the basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls with a defensive enclosure called Johannipolis.

He also tried to break the alliances between Saracens and the southern Italian cities of Naples, Gaeta, and Amalfi, and at times paid tribute to buy peace. His letters, hundreds of which survive in the papal register, reveal his constant appeals for aid.

Methodius, archbishop in Moravia, had been imprisoned by Frankish bishops who objected to his mission. John secured his release in 873. In 880, after examining Methodius in Rome, he issued the letter Industriae tuae, which confirmed his orthodoxy and allowed the liturgy to be celebrated in Slavonic, with the Gospel read first in Latin.

When Patriarch Ignatius died in 877, Photius returned to office. John accepted his restoration, and papal legates attended a council in Constantinople in 879 and 880 that recognized him. Western and Eastern accounts later disagreed over exactly what John approved.

John died in December 882. The Annals of Fulda report that a relative, hoping to seize his treasure, poisoned him and then, when the poison worked too slowly, struck him with a hammer. No other contemporary source gives details, but on that account he is often described as the first pope to be assassinated.

keyFacts: Crowned Charles the Bald (875) and Charles the Fat (881) as emperors
Built a papal fleet and fortified St. Paul's as Johannipolis
Issued Industriae tuae (880) permitting the Slavonic liturgy
Recognized Photius as patriarch at the council of 879–880
Murdered in December 882, according to the Annals of Fulda

faqs.question: Was John VIII the first pope to be murdered?
faqs.answer: He is commonly described that way. The Annals of Fulda say he was poisoned and then beaten to death by a relative in 882. Earlier popes died as martyrs or in exile, but John VIII is the first recorded victim of assassination.

faqs.question: What did John VIII decide about the Slavonic liturgy?
faqs.answer: In 880 he approved Methodius's teaching and allowed the Mass to be celebrated in Slavonic, provided the Gospel was first read in Latin.

faqs.question: Which emperors did John VIII crown?
faqs.answer: Charles the Bald on Christmas Day 875 and Charles the Fat in 881.

directAnswer: Pope Marinus I, a native of Gallese and son of a priest, reigned from 882 to 884. An experienced papal legate, he was already bishop of Caere when elected, making him the first bishop of another see to become pope. He reversed the condemnation of Formosus and maintained friendly ties with King Alfred of Wessex.

paras: Marinus entered the clergy as a boy and served the Roman Church on several missions to Constantinople. He was one of the papal legates at the Fourth Council of Constantinople in 869 and 870, where Photius was condemned.

He had been made bishop of Caere (modern Cerveteri). Church custom then opposed moving a bishop from one see to another, so his election marked a notable break with precedent, one later invoked in the controversy over Formosus.

Marinus lifted the sentences that John VIII had passed in 876 on Formosus of Porto and others, restoring Formosus to his diocese. He is also reported to have renewed the condemnation of Photius, though details are limited.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that he exempted the English quarter in Rome, the Schola Saxonum, from taxation at King Alfred's request and sent Alfred a relic of the True Cross. He died in May 884. Some older lists wrongly call him Martin II, a confusion of the two names in medieval copies.

keyFacts: Born at Gallese, son of a priest
Papal legate at the Fourth Council of Constantinople (869–870)
First bishop of another diocese (Caere) to be elected pope
Restored Formosus to the see of Porto
Sent a relic of the True Cross to King Alfred of Wessex

faqs.question: Why is Marinus I sometimes called Martin II?
faqs.answer: Medieval scribes confused the names Marinus and Martinus. Because of that error, the later Pope Martin who took office in 1281 is numbered Martin IV, even though only one earlier Martin was pope.

faqs.question: What was unusual about Marinus I's election?
faqs.answer: He was already bishop of Caere. Moving a bishop to another see was then discouraged by church law, so his election was a significant precedent.

faqs.question: How was Marinus I connected to Alfred the Great?
faqs.answer: According to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, he freed the English quarter in Rome from taxes at Alfred's request and sent him a relic of the True Cross.

directAnswer: Pope St. Adrian III was a Roman who reigned for about fourteen months, from 884 to 885. Few details of his pontificate survive; he died near Modena while traveling to meet Emperor Charles the Fat and was buried in the abbey of Nonantola, where he has long been venerated. Pope Leo XIII confirmed his cult in 1891.

paras: Adrian was the son of a Roman named Benedict, and there is a tradition that Adrian I was among his ancestors, though this is uncertain. He became pope during the factional strife that followed John VIII's murder. Fragmentary sources say he punished severely some of those involved in Roman conspiracies, including a high official who was blinded, but the circumstances are poorly documented and historians treat these reports with caution.
He is also said to have sent a letter of communion to Photius in Constantinople and to have helped relieve a famine in Rome, but these points too rest on limited evidence.

sections.h2: Death at San Cesario and Veneration at Nonantola
paras: In 885 Emperor Charles the Fat summoned Adrian to a diet at Worms, apparently to settle the question of the imperial succession. On the journey north Adrian fell ill and died near San Cesario sul Panaro, in the territory of Modena. He was buried at the nearby Benedictine abbey of Nonantola.
Local devotion grew around his tomb, and miracles were attributed to his intercession. In 1891 Pope Leo XIII confirmed his longstanding cult. His feast is kept on July 8.

keyFacts: Roman by birth, son of Benedict
Reigned about fourteen months (884–885)
Died near Modena on the way to an imperial diet at Worms
Buried at the abbey of Nonantola
Cult confirmed by Leo XIII in 1891; feast July 8

faqs.question: Why is Adrian III a saint?
faqs.answer: Devotion arose at his tomb in the abbey of Nonantola, where miracles were reported. Pope Leo XIII formally confirmed this ancient cult in 1891.

faqs.question: Where did Pope Adrian III die?
faqs.answer: Near San Cesario sul Panaro, close to Modena, while traveling to meet Emperor Charles the Fat in 885.

directAnswer: Pope Stephen V, a Roman nobleman, reigned from 885 to 891. He used his family wealth to relieve famine in Rome, forbade the Slavonic liturgy after the death of St. Methodius, and crowned Guy of Spoleto emperor in 891. He is sometimes numbered Stephen VI.

paras: Stephen was raised by his relative Bishop Zachary, the papal librarian, and rose through the Roman clergy to become a cardinal priest. He was consecrated without waiting for imperial confirmation; Emperor Charles the Fat objected at first but accepted the election after receiving the decree.

According to the Liber Pontificalis, he found the papal treasury and storehouses nearly empty when he took office, and he drew on his family's fortune to feed Romans during a time of drought and hunger. After Charles the Fat was deposed in 887, Stephen eventually turned to Guy of Spoleto, whom he crowned emperor in 891.

sections.h2: The End of the Moravian Slavonic Mission
paras: After St. Methodius died in 885, his Frankish rival Wiching gained influence in Moravia. A letter attributed to Stephen forbade the celebration of the liturgy in Slavonic. Methodius's disciples were expelled; several found refuge in Bulgaria, where Slavonic Christian culture took root and flourished.
Stephen also wrote to Archbishop Liutbert of Mainz rejecting trials by ordeal as a means of proving guilt. He died in September 891.

keyFacts: Roman noble educated by his kinsman, the papal librarian Zachary
Relieved famine in Rome with his family's wealth
Banned the Slavonic liturgy in Moravia after Methodius died (885)
Crowned Guy of Spoleto emperor in 891
Sometimes numbered Stephen VI

faqs.question: Why did Stephen V forbid the Slavonic liturgy?
faqs.answer: After Methodius died, his Frankish opponents in Moravia gained the upper hand, and a papal letter under Stephen V prohibited the Slavonic rite. Methodius's disciples then carried their work to Bulgaria.

faqs.question: Whom did Stephen V crown emperor?
faqs.answer: Guy, duke of Spoleto, in 891, after the collapse of Charles the Fat's rule.

directAnswer: Pope Formosus, previously bishop of Porto and a papal legate to Bulgaria, reigned from 891 to 896. He crowned two rival emperors, Lambert of Spoleto and Arnulf of Carinthia, amid the collapse of the Carolingian order. Months after his death his corpse was put on trial by Stephen VI at the notorious Cadaver Synod, a verdict later overturned.

paras: Formosus was made bishop of Porto, one of the dioceses near Rome, by Nicholas I in 864. Two years later Nicholas sent him as a legate to Bulgaria, whose ruler Boris I had just accepted Christianity. Formosus worked there with such success that Boris asked to have him as archbishop of Bulgaria. Nicholas refused, since the canons of the time forbade transferring a bishop from one see to another.
He later served on missions to the Frankish kingdoms and was widely regarded as able and personally austere. His contemporaries, friend and foe alike, did not accuse him of moral laxity.

Under John VIII, Formosus became entangled in Roman factional politics. In 876 he fled the city, and a synod condemned him on charges that included deserting his diocese and conspiring against the pope; he was excommunicated and later required to swear never to return to Rome or exercise priestly office.

Pope Marinus I lifted these penalties in 883 and restored him to Porto. When Formosus was elected pope in October 891, his opponents argued that, as bishop of another see, he could not lawfully be translated to Rome, an argument that would be used against him after his death.

Formosus inherited Emperor Guy of Spoleto, crowned by Stephen V, and in 892 he crowned Guy's son Lambert as co-emperor. The pope distrusted Spoletan power, however, and appealed to Arnulf of Carinthia, the East Frankish king, to come to Italy.

Arnulf took Rome in February 896 and was crowned emperor by Formosus, but he was soon struck by paralysis and withdrew north. Formosus died on April 4, 896, leaving Rome exposed to the Spoletan party he had opposed.

sections.h2: The Cadaver Synod and Its Reversal
paras: In January 897 Stephen VI, probably under pressure from the Spoletan faction, had the body of Formosus exhumed, dressed in papal vestments, and seated in court at the Lateran. A deacon answered on the dead man's behalf. The synod declared Formosus's election invalid because of his translation from Porto, annulled his acts and ordinations, cut off the fingers of his right hand used for blessing, and eventually threw the body into the Tiber.

The macabre trial provoked revulsion in Rome. The body was recovered, and Theodore II gave it honorable burial in St. Peter's later in 897. John IX's synods in 898 annulled the Cadaver Synod and forbade trials of the dead, though Sergius III later revived the condemnation of Formosus's ordinations for a time.

keyFacts: Bishop of Porto from 864 and papal legate to Bulgaria in 866
Excommunicated under John VIII (876), restored by Marinus I (883)
Crowned Lambert of Spoleto (892) and Arnulf of Carinthia (896) emperors
Died April 4, 896
Tried posthumously at the Cadaver Synod in January 897; reburied in St. Peter's later that year

faqs.question: Why was Pope Formosus put on trial after his death?
faqs.answer: His enemies, especially the Spoletan faction, wanted his acts and the imperial coronation of Arnulf declared invalid. Stephen VI tried his corpse in 897, charging that he had unlawfully moved from the see of Porto to Rome.

faqs.question: Was the Cadaver Synod's verdict ever overturned?
faqs.answer: Yes. Theodore II reburied Formosus with honor in 897, and synods under John IX in 898 annulled the Cadaver Synod and prohibited any future trial of a dead person.

faqs.question: Why did Bulgaria's ruler want Formosus?
faqs.answer: As papal legate in 866, Formosus impressed Boris I so much that Boris asked for him as archbishop of Bulgaria. Nicholas I declined because church law then barred moving a bishop to a new see.

directAnswer: Pope Boniface VI was a Roman cleric who held the papacy for only about fifteen days in April 896, immediately after the death of Formosus. He had previously been degraded from holy orders twice under John VIII, and a later synod under John IX declared his election invalid. Very little else is known about him.

sections.h2: Elected in the Turmoil After Formosus
paras: Boniface was the son of a Roman named Hadrian. Under John VIII he had been deposed first from the subdiaconate and then from the priesthood for misconduct, though the sources do not specify the offenses. When Formosus died in April 896, a popular uprising in Rome secured his election, apparently over the objections of the more cautious clergy.
He died about two weeks later; the traditional account attributes his death to gout. Nothing in the sources records any acts of his brief pontificate.

At the Roman synod held by John IX in 898, the bishops ruled that Boniface's election had been unlawful because of his earlier depositions, and forbade that such a choice ever be repeated. Despite this, he has remained in the official list of popes, a sign of how unsettled the rules of legitimacy were during these years of faction and violence.

keyFacts: Roman, son of Hadrian
Reigned about fifteen days in April 896
Twice deposed from holy orders under John VIII
His election was condemned by John IX's synod in 898

faqs.question: How long was Boniface VI pope?
faqs.answer: About fifteen days in April 896, one of the shortest pontificates on record.

faqs.question: Why was Boniface VI's election condemned?
faqs.answer: He had been deposed from the subdiaconate and the priesthood under John VIII. A synod under John IX in 898 judged that such a man could not lawfully be elected pope.

directAnswer: Pope Stephen VI, previously bishop of Anagni, reigned from May 896 to August 897. He is remembered almost entirely for the Cadaver Synod, at which he had the exhumed body of his predecessor Formosus tried and condemned. Public outrage followed, and Stephen was imprisoned and strangled. He is sometimes numbered Stephen VII.

sections.h2: Bishop of Anagni and Partisan of Spoleto
paras: Stephen was the son of a Roman priest named John. Formosus himself had consecrated him bishop of Anagni, and like Formosus he was therefore translated from another see when he became pope in May 896. Stephen appears to have been closely aligned with the house of Spoleto, the emperor Lambert and his mother Ageltrude, who bitterly resented Formosus for crowning their rival Arnulf.
Historians generally believe Spoletan pressure lay behind what followed, though the sources do not reveal Stephen's own motives in detail.

In January 897 Stephen convened a synod in the Lateran. The body of Formosus, dead for about nine months, was exhumed, clothed in pontifical vestments, and placed on a throne, while a deacon was appointed to reply for him. Stephen presided and questioned the corpse himself.

The synod found Formosus guilty of having unlawfully left the see of Porto for Rome, declared his pontificate void, and annulled all the ordinations he had performed. The three fingers of his right hand used in blessing were cut off, and the body was buried in a common grave and later cast into the Tiber. By invalidating Formosus's ordinations, the synod also conveniently voided Stephen's own consecration as bishop of Anagni, removing the canonical obstacle to his election.

Shortly afterward the Lateran basilica collapsed, probably as a result of an earthquake, and many Romans saw it as a sign of divine displeasure. Reports that Formosus's body had worked miracles stirred popular feeling further.

In the summer of 897 a revolt broke out. Stephen was seized, stripped of his papal insignia, and imprisoned, and in August he was strangled in his cell. His successors Theodore II and John IX overturned his synod, and the episode remains one of the darkest in papal history.

keyFacts: Former bishop of Anagni, consecrated by Formosus
Presided over the Cadaver Synod in January 897
The Lateran basilica collapsed soon after the synod
Imprisoned and strangled in August 897
Sometimes numbered Stephen VII

faqs.question: What was the Cadaver Synod?
faqs.answer: A synod held by Stephen VI in January 897 at which the exhumed body of Pope Formosus was put on trial, convicted, mutilated, and stripped of its papal status.

faqs.question: How did Stephen VI die?
faqs.answer: After popular outrage over the Cadaver Synod, a revolt in Rome led to his imprisonment, and he was strangled in prison in August 897.

faqs.question: Why might Stephen VI have wanted Formosus condemned?
faqs.answer: Political pressure from the Spoletan family is the most likely reason. Annulling Formosus's ordinations also removed the objection that Stephen himself had been moved from the see of Anagni.

directAnswer: Pope Romanus, a native of Gallese and cardinal priest of San Pietro in Vincoli, reigned for roughly three months in 897, after the fall of Stephen VI. He is generally thought to have sympathized with the memory of Formosus, but his acts are poorly documented, and how his pontificate ended is uncertain.

paras: Romanus came from Gallese, the same town as Marinus I, and was the son of a man named Constantine. He was elected in the late summer of 897, after the revolt that overthrew Stephen VI. Many historians believe he belonged to the party that wished to rehabilitate Formosus, though the formal annulment of the Cadaver Synod is credited to his successors Theodore II and John IX.

A few documents from his reign survive, including grants of privileges to churches, among them sees in Spain and the patriarchate of Grado. They show the ordinary business of the papal chancery continuing even amid the upheaval.

Romanus ceased to be pope in November 897. Some later accounts say he was deposed and lived out his life as a monk, but the evidence is thin, and the exact reason his reign ended is not known. His brief pontificate is a reminder of how little the sources reveal about many popes of this troubled decade.

keyFacts: Born at Gallese, son of Constantine
Cardinal priest of San Pietro in Vincoli
Reigned about three months in 897
Possibly deposed and made a monk, though this is uncertain

faqs.question: Did Pope Romanus annul the Cadaver Synod?
faqs.answer: He is thought to have favored Formosus's memory, but the formal annulment is attributed to Theodore II and especially John IX.

faqs.question: How did Romanus's pontificate end?
faqs.answer: No one knows for certain. Later tradition says he was deposed and became a monk, but contemporary evidence is lacking.

directAnswer: Pope Theodore II was a Roman priest who reigned for only about twenty days in December 897. In that short time he held a synod that reinstated the clergy ordained by Formosus and gave the body of Formosus, recovered from the Tiber, an honorable burial in St. Peter's.

paras: Theodore was the son of a Roman named Photius and had a brother named Theodosius. The sources describe him as a man of peace and generosity. Elected after the obscure end of Romanus's pontificate, he quickly convened a synod that annulled the decisions of the Cadaver Synod and restored to office the bishops and priests whom Formosus had ordained and Stephen VI had deposed.
Formosus's body had been pulled from the Tiber, reportedly by a monk, and kept in hiding. Theodore had it brought back and buried in St. Peter's, dressed in pontifical vestments.

sections.h2: A Legend and a Sudden Death
paras: Liutprand of Cremona, writing decades later, relates that as Formosus's body was carried into St. Peter's, images of the saints bowed in reverence. This is a legend reflecting popular sympathy for the wronged pope, not a documented event.
Theodore died after about twenty days in office; the cause of his death is not recorded. His work was confirmed and expanded by John IX the following year.

keyFacts: Roman, son of a man named Photius
Reigned about twenty days in December 897
Held a synod reinstating clergy ordained by Formosus
Reburied Formosus in St. Peter's

faqs.question: What did Theodore II do for Pope Formosus?
faqs.answer: He held a synod that reversed the Cadaver Synod's actions against Formosus's clergy and had Formosus's recovered body solemnly buried in St. Peter's.

faqs.question: How did Theodore II die?
faqs.answer: The sources say only that he died after about twenty days as pope; no cause is recorded.

directAnswer: Pope John IX was a Benedictine monk from Tivoli who reigned from 898 to 900. Through synods at Rome and Ravenna he formally annulled the Cadaver Synod, rehabilitated Formosus, banned trials of the dead, and required that papal consecrations take place in the presence of imperial envoys.

paras: John, the son of Rampoald, had been a monk of the Order of St. Benedict and was ordained priest by Formosus. After Theodore II's death, a faction hostile to Formosus put forward Sergius, later Pope Sergius III, but John's supporters prevailed, and he soon worked closely with Emperor Lambert. Sergius and his allies were excommunicated and driven from Rome.

Early in 898 John held a synod in Rome that confirmed Theodore II's decisions. It declared the acts of the Cadaver Synod void, ordered its records burned, restored the clergy ordained by Formosus, and prohibited the trial of anyone after death. It also condemned the irregular election of Boniface VI.

To prevent the violence that had marred recent elections, the synod decreed that a new pope should be consecrated only in the presence of imperial representatives. A second synod at Ravenna, held with Emperor Lambert, confirmed these measures and the rights of the Roman Church. Lambert's death later that year deprived John of a protector, and he also had to reckon with Hungarian raids in northern Italy. John died in January 900.

keyFacts: Born at Tivoli; a Benedictine monk ordained by Formosus
Elected over the rival candidate Sergius (later Sergius III)
Held synods at Rome and Ravenna in 898
Annulled the Cadaver Synod and forbade trials of the dead
Required imperial envoys at papal consecrations

faqs.question: How did John IX respond to the Cadaver Synod?
faqs.answer: His Roman synod of 898 declared it void, ordered its records destroyed, restored Formosus's clergy, and banned any future trial of a dead person.

faqs.question: Who was John IX's rival for the papacy?
faqs.answer: Sergius, an opponent of Formosus, was proposed by a rival faction in 898. He was excommunicated and exiled, but later became pope as Sergius III.

directAnswer: Pope Benedict IV was a Roman priest who reigned from 900 to 903. He crowned Louis of Provence emperor in 901 and excommunicated the murderers of Archbishop Fulk of Reims. Later writers praised his generosity, but the record of his pontificate is slight, and even the exact end date is uncertain.

sections.h2: A Formosan Priest Who Became Pope
paras: Benedict was a Roman, the son of a man named Mammolus, and had been ordained priest by Formosus. His election in early 900 thus signaled the continuing dominance of the party that had restored Formosus's memory. The tenth-century historian Flodoard of Reims commended him for his kindness to the poor and his concern for the common good.
In 900 he excommunicated the men who had murdered Fulk, archbishop of Reims, a crime connected to the feuds of the Flemish count Baldwin II.

sections.h2: The Coronation of Louis of Provence
paras: After the death of Lambert of Spoleto, Italy lacked an emperor. Louis of Provence, a grandson of Emperor Louis II through his mother, came south and was crowned emperor by Benedict in Rome in 901. His rule proved short-lived; in 905 his rival Berengar captured and blinded him, which is why he is remembered as Louis the Blind.
Benedict died in the summer of 903 and was buried in St. Peter's. Beyond these few events, little survives about him.

keyFacts: Roman, son of Mammolus; ordained priest by Formosus
Excommunicated the murderers of Archbishop Fulk of Reims (900)
Crowned Louis of Provence emperor in 901
Praised by Flodoard of Reims for his charity

faqs.question: Which emperor did Benedict IV crown?
faqs.answer: Louis of Provence, in 901. Louis was later blinded by his rival Berengar and is known as Louis the Blind.

faqs.question: Why is Benedict IV well regarded despite the period's turmoil?
faqs.answer: The chronicler Flodoard of Reims praised his generosity to the poor and his devotion to the public good, though few details of his reign survive.

directAnswer: Pope Leo V was a priest from Ardea, south of Rome, who reigned for about a month or two in 903. He was overthrown and imprisoned by Christopher, a priest who then claimed the papacy and is listed as an antipope. Both men appear to have died in custody, though the details are uncertain.

sections.h2: A Priest From Outside the Roman Clergy
paras: Leo was not one of the cardinal clergy of Rome but a priest serving at Ardea, which made his election unusual. The reasons for his choice are unknown, though it may have been an attempt to find a candidate outside the city's rival factions. Auxilius, a writer who defended Formosus's ordinations, later spoke of Leo as a man of holy life.
No acts of his pontificate are securely documented.

Within weeks, Christopher, cardinal priest of San Damaso, seized power, threw Leo into prison, and took the papal office himself. Christopher is regarded as an antipope. In early 904 he too was removed when Sergius III entered Rome.

Several sources say that both Leo and Christopher were killed in prison, and some attribute their deaths to Sergius III, but the evidence is fragmentary and partly hostile, and historians do not agree on what happened.

keyFacts: A priest of Ardea, not a member of the Roman cardinal clergy
Reigned about one to two months in 903
Deposed and imprisoned by the antipope Christopher
Probably died in prison; circumstances uncertain

faqs.question: Who overthrew Pope Leo V?
faqs.answer: Christopher, a Roman cardinal priest, who imprisoned Leo and claimed the papacy. Christopher is now counted as an antipope.

faqs.question: Was Leo V murdered?
faqs.answer: Some sources report that he was killed in prison, possibly under Sergius III, but the accounts are fragmentary and the matter remains uncertain.

directAnswer: Pope Sergius III was a Roman nobleman who reigned from 904 to 911. A fierce opponent of Formosus, he renewed the condemnation of Formosus's ordinations, rebuilt the Lateran basilica, and relied on the powerful Roman family of Theophylact. His pontificate is often taken as the start of the period historians call the saeculum obscurum, the dark age of the papacy.

paras: Sergius came from a noble Roman family and had been made bishop of Caere by Formosus, an ordination he later rejected. In 898, after the death of Theodore II, a party hostile to Formosus put him forward for the papacy, but John IX prevailed. Sergius was excommunicated and spent about seven years in exile.

In early 904, with armed support, he returned to Rome, removed the antipope Christopher, and was consecrated. His pontificate rested heavily on the backing of Theophylact, a leading Roman official, and his wife Theodora, whose family dominated the city for decades.

Sergius declared the acts of Formosus void once more and required clergy ordained by Formosus or his supporters to be re-ordained, causing widespread confusion and anguish. Defenders of Formosus, such as the writers Auxilius and Eugenius Vulgarius, protested in treatises that survive.
He also rebuilt the Lateran basilica, which had collapsed in the time of Stephen VI, restoring the cathedral of Rome after years of ruin.

In the East, Emperor Leo VI sought approval for his fourth marriage, which Byzantine church law condemned. Papal legates sent by Sergius granted a dispensation, and the patriarch Nicholas Mystikos, who opposed the marriage, was removed for a time. The affair caused lasting resentment in Constantinople.

In 910, during Sergius's reign, Duke William of Aquitaine founded the abbey of Cluny and placed it directly under the protection of the Apostles Peter and Paul and the Roman pontiff. Cluny would become a leading force in the reform of the Church in later generations.

The sixteenth-century historian Cardinal Baronius used the phrase saeculum obscurum for the era of Roman aristocratic control that Sergius's reign is often said to begin. Liutprand of Cremona, writing some decades later, claimed Sergius fathered a son, the future John XI, with Theophylact's daughter Marozia. Liutprand was a hostile and gossipy witness, and historians remain divided on the claim. Sergius died in April 911.

keyFacts: Formerly bishop of Caere, ordained by Formosus
Rival candidate to John IX in 898; in exile until 904
Renewed the condemnation of Formosus's ordinations
Rebuilt the Lateran basilica
Cluny Abbey was founded under papal protection in 910 during his reign

faqs.question: What is the saeculum obscurum?
faqs.answer: A term coined by Cardinal Baronius for the period, often dated from Sergius III's reign, when Roman aristocratic families controlled papal elections.

faqs.question: How did Sergius III treat the memory of Formosus?
faqs.answer: He reversed the rehabilitation granted by Theodore II and John IX, declared Formosus's ordinations invalid, and required affected clergy to be re-ordained.

faqs.question: Is it true that Sergius III was the father of Pope John XI?
faqs.answer: The claim comes from Liutprand of Cremona, a later and hostile writer. It cannot be confirmed, and historians disagree about it.

directAnswer: Pope Anastasius III was a Roman who reigned for about two years, from 911 to 913, during the ascendancy of Theophylact's family in Rome. The sources describe him as mild and upright, but they record very few acts of his pontificate.

sections.h2: A Quiet Pontificate in the Theophylact Era
paras: Anastasius was the son of a Roman named Lucian. He was elected after the death of Sergius III, at a time when the senator Theophylact and his family held effective control over the city, and it is generally assumed that his election had their approval.
Chroniclers such as Flodoard speak well of his character, but the surviving record consists mainly of a few privileges granted to churches and monasteries.

sections.h2: Echoes of the Byzantine Marriage Dispute
paras: The Byzantine controversy over Emperor Leo VI's fourth marriage continued into Anastasius's time. After Leo's death, Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos wrote to Rome protesting the dispensation granted under Sergius III, but no clear papal response survives.
Anastasius died around June 913 and was buried in St. Peter's. Little more is known about him, and his pontificate is remembered chiefly as a calm interval in a turbulent age.

keyFacts: Roman, son of Lucian
Reigned about two years (911–913)
Pope during the dominance of Theophylact's family in Rome
Buried in St. Peter's

faqs.question: Why is so little known about Anastasius III?
faqs.answer: His pontificate was short and occurred during a period when Roman records are sparse. Only a handful of documents and brief mentions by chroniclers survive.

faqs.question: Who held power in Rome during Anastasius III's reign?
faqs.answer: The family of the senator Theophylact and his wife Theodora, who dominated Roman politics in the early tenth century.
